props.title: Live music on your calendar, every week.
props.lede: You know the moment on a quiet night when your guests start asking for the check. A musician on your floor can give them a reason to stay for one more round.

headingText.html: We bring the same solo or duo act to your lobby bar, restaurant or lounge on the same night each week. We also book single dates for lobby events and the holidays.

rows.text: A Colorado act you've watched on video plays at your venue every week, so your regulars get to know them.
If your musician can't make it, we'll send an act you've already approved. If we can't fill the night, you aren't billed for it. This is part of the Backup Promise.

rows.term: A different act if the first one isn't right
rows.text: Just tell us, and we'll bring in another act from our roster.

rows.term: Extra nights when you want them
rows.text: We can add a holiday night, a bigger act for a special evening, or a seasonal act like the Christmas jazz trio or the mariachi band.
The act brings a small sound system and keeps the music low enough that your guests can still talk.
We bill on the 1st for that month's nights, due in 30 days, and we'll send a certificate of insurance naming your property.

props.title: Guests stay longer to slower songs

props.html: Guests stayed at the table about 23 minutes longer when the songs were slow.
In 2024, researchers at an Italian restaurant in Tel Aviv changed the tempo of the background music and timed 282 tables. They kept the same food, the same staff and the same prices.

props.caption: Average minutes at the table, 282 tables, one Italian restaurant in Tel Aviv, 2024.

props.html: In a 1986 study at an American restaurant, guests on slow-music nights ordered more drinks. A live musician can also watch who’s at the bar and pick the next song for them, which a playlist can’t do.
You can read the full research, with every source, in our post on why restaurants have live music.

items.a: Most venues start with one night, like a weeknight in the lobby bar or restaurant, or a weekend brunch. You pick the day and the time.

items.q: How long does the musician play?
items.a: They play for three hours, in three 50-minute sets. We can keep recorded music going during the breaks if you'd like.

items.q: What do you need from us?
items.a: We'll need a corner about 6 by 4 feet, one outlet, a stool, and about 45 minutes to set up before the first set.

items.q: What if we need to cancel a night?
items.a: Tell us 14 or more days ahead and you aren't billed for it. With less notice, the night is still billed.

items.q: What happens on the patio when the weather turns?
items.a: The musician moves inside, or plays a shorter night if you'd rather.
Yes. You'll get one invoice on the 1st of each month, due in 30 days. The first month is paid before the first night. We can set up as a vendor and work from a purchase order.

items.q: Do we need a license for live music?
items.a: Yes, and it's the venue that holds it. Live music is covered by public performance licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR, and many hotels already have them. A license for background music, or one that comes with a music service, may not cover a live musician, so it's worth checking with each of them before the first night.

items.q: Does the musician put out a tip jar?
items.a: The musician only puts one out if you'd like one.
We quote per night after a conversation, based on the act and the nights you want.
